$comment: Machine-readable index of the examples. Written for agents deciding which example to copy. Human version: ./README.md
verificationNote: Pinned examples passed isolated installation, typecheck, math tests and build. Examples 09 and 10 were also reproduced locally with a supplied public token against real Mapbox tiles on 2026-09-06. Recorded screenshots retain their historical provenance; see docs/demo-implementation-plan.md for the exact browser scope and remaining gates.

conventions.selfContained: Each example has its own package.json and node_modules and imports nothing outside its own folder. Duplicated files between examples are intentional. Copy a whole folder rather than importing across.
conventions.token: Standalone examples read import.meta.env.VITE_MAPBOX_TOKEN. In demo embed mode, selected native and custom examples accept a runtime public token only from the same-origin parent. No token is committed; site builds use an empty envDir.
conventions.acceptance: npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm run test --if-present && npm run build. The gallery has no math tests. Browser behavior is a separate gate.

statusMarkers.verified: Runs in production and is reproduced by an example here
statusMarkers.reported: Runs in production, not reproduced here
statusMarkers.unverified: Reasoned from source or typings, never run

siteScenes.fixture: three locally generated schematic circular orbits

accepted: closed pre-sampled paths with longitudeDeg, latitudeDeg, altitudeMeters, and an optional satelliteAt(simSec) marker provider
inputContract.missingData: Reject non-finite coordinates or altitude; do not coerce missing altitude to the Earth surface.

acceptance.en: Use a non-fixture orbit set. Verify closed elevated paths, inclination, animated markers, high-altitude visibility beyond the surface horizon, antimeridian continuity, pause/resume, and globe-to-Mercator transition.
acceptance.zh-TW: 使用一組非內建 fixture 的軌道資料，驗證閉合離地路徑、傾角、移動標記、高空越過地表地平線後的可見性、換日線連續性、暫停／播放與 globe-to-Mercator 過渡。

siteScenes.fixture: locally authored illustrative Taiwan-area ADIZ schematic

inputContract.heightUnit: metres; a display property, never an inferred legal ceiling
inputContract.missingData: Reject empty rings, non-finite coordinates, and coordinates outside the supported Web Mercator latitude range.
inputContract.notIncluded: authoritative ADIZ data, sovereignty, airspace classification, or a solid top fill

acceptance.en: Use a non-ADIZ Polygon or MultiPolygon. Verify exterior and interior rings form subdivided bottom-to-top side walls without a top fill, remain continuous at the antimeridian, survive remove/re-add, and never present display height as a legal ceiling.
acceptance.zh-TW: 使用一組非 ADIZ 的 Polygon 或 MultiPolygon，驗證外環與內環都形成經細分、由底至頂的側牆且沒有頂蓋，跨換日線仍連續、移除後可重新掛載，並且不把顯示高度描述成法定上限。

examples.title: Glowing points that hug the globe
examples.settles: The core projection recipe plus the spark/glow shader. The flagship example — start here.

knobs.effect: Recolors each airport from a separate deterministic synthetic color hash; it does not encode a real category.
Global multiplier on gl_PointSize.
Layer alpha before additive blending.
How far each point's centre is pushed toward white. 0 keeps the source colour; high values read as a light source.

teaches: The render arguments the public typings under-document, and what each is for.
Precomputing ECEF per vertex, and blending sphere to plane with a four-line mix() in the vertex shader.
Why every material needs depthTest:false in globe projection, and why the far side must then be culled in ECEF space.
Three-band radial halo plus additive blending as a substitute for post-process bloom.

verifiedStates.note: on the sphere, far side culled
mid-blend, points still registered on their cities

examples.title: Great-circle arcs, and why lines cut through the planet
examples.settles: Lines spanning long distances. Subdivision is the subject: the slider goes down to 2 so the failure is reproducible on demand.

knobs.effect: Vertices per arc, not segments per arc. At 2 each arc is a chord straight through the planet — that is the bug this example exists to show.
Peak radial offset at the arc midpoint. Real cruising altitude is about 0.16% of Earth's radius and invisible; this is deliberate exaggeration.
Assigns stable synthetic per-route colors for visual separation; colors do not encode route categories or traffic.

teaches: Vertices are projected, the segments between them are not. Subdivide anything spanning distance.
Use slerp, not linear interpolation of lon/lat: linear interpolation does not jump, it smoothly goes the wrong way round.
Antipodal pairs need a separate branch (Rodrigues rotation) to avoid dividing by sin(pi).
MercatorCoordinate.fromLngLat is not periodic, so longitude must be resolved per segment, not per vertex.

data.note: 20 hand-picked hubs; the 190 O-D pairs are synthetic, not real routes.

examples.title: Filled areas and outlines on a sphere
examples.settles: Polygons, coverage circles and bounding boxes. Also: a fixed-radius circle is a small circle on a sphere and looks different at every latitude.

knobs.effect: Subdivision per edge. Low values turn circles into visible polygons and bbox edges into chords.
Geodesic radius of all three demo circles. Above the distance to the pole, the near-polar circle wraps the pole and its boundary appears on the opposite meridian.
Which generators are drawn.

teaches: Polygon edges are chords too — subdivide them like any other line.
A geodesic circle is a small circle; its screen shape varies with latitude and viewing angle.
asin() needs clamping near the pole: floating point can push its argument past 1 and return NaN.
At a few hundred vertices you do not need a shader — projecting on the CPU each frame is easier to read and costs nothing measurable.
limitations: Fan triangulation only, so concave polygons and holes are not supported (no earcut dependency).
Bounding boxes crossing the antimeridian interpolate the long way round; not detected, not split.
A circle large enough to enclose a pole will self-intersect under fan triangulation.

examples.title: Objects moving along paths, with timeline playback
examples.settles: Geometry whose position changes every frame — the branch where ECEF cannot be precomputed and must be derived in the vertex shader.

knobs.effect: Active object count via setDrawRange. Capacity is fixed at 50; objects are never created or destroyed.
Fade window in the shader, not ring-buffer capacity. Capacity is fixed at 150 samples.
Simulation time multiplier.
Head point size multiplier.
Layer alpha.
Timeline position as a percentage. Scrubbing backwards is supported: position is a pure function of time, not accumulated state.

teaches: Deriving ECEF in the vertex shader with an inverse Mercator, for vertices that have no fixed position to precompute.
Six transcendental calls per vertex per frame is the cost, and the transition early-out means you pay none of it on a flat map.
Ring-buffer trails indexed by simulation tick, so scrubbing backwards is deterministic.
Uploading only the changed range of a buffer instead of rebuilding the geometry.
limitations: Trails are point clouds rather than continuous lines, which sidesteps the guard-vertex problem in docs/03-scaling-up/batched-trails.md.
Trail vertices are frozen once written but still take the shader-derivation path every frame; the production optimisation is to precompute them on write.
No object eviction — a scenario with a changing population needs the min-heap approach in docs/03-scaling-up/batched-trails.md.

examples.title: Thousands of trajectories in one draw call
examples.settles: What to do when per-object buffer updates stop scaling. Fixed slot pool, guard vertices, partial uploads, min-heap eviction.

knobs.effect: Active object count. Capacity is fixed at 4,096 slots, so beyond that objects compete and the losers get evicted.
Eviction strategy. Switch it live and read ms/update — this comparison is the example's whole point.
Simulation rate.
Layer alpha.
Per-object trail colors, retained in light and dark themes; shader uniform switch without rebuilding trail buffers.

measured.scenario: 5,000 objects against a 4,096-slot pool, in a browser
measured.nodeMicrobench: 3,000 objects / 1,024 slots: heap 16.81 ms per call vs linear scan 277.92 ms — about 16.5x on the eviction step alone, undiluted by the rest of the frame

teaches: One THREE.Line plus a fixed slot pool keeps the draw call count at 1 regardless of object count.
Guard vertices isolate slots; without them a line strip connects one object's tail to the next one's head.
Upload only the changed range per attribute instead of rebuilding the geometry.
A min-heap replaces an O(capacity) scan for the oldest slot — the single change that turns a CPU-bound frame into a GPU-bound one.
limitations: Forward playback only: eviction reshuffles the population non-deterministically, so scrubbing backwards would mean replaying the whole eviction history.
Line width is about 1px — most drivers ignore lineWidth on THREE.Line.

examples.title: Vector field particles, in raw WebGL2
examples.settles: Wind and ocean-current streaks when the native raster-particle layer does not fit — your data is not in raster-array format, it updates in real time, or you are on MapLibre.

knobs.effect: Base count. At low zoom the adaptive density multiplies it, so the number you set is not the number you get.
Samples kept per particle. Multiplies segments per frame.
Advection rate. Particle lifetime is a frame counter rather than simulation seconds, so raising speed does not shorten lifetimes.
Fat-line width in pixels.
Layer alpha.
Uncheck to watch ms/update stay elevated as the backing buffer reallocates on nearly every frame instead of only at quantum steps.

measured.renderer: SwiftShader software renderer, no GPU — treat these as an upper bound on real hardware

teaches: CPU-side Euler advection with a clamped frame dt, so a backgrounded tab does not fling every particle on return.
Instanced fat lines: 8 floats per segment instead of six vertices of ten floats.
Quantize zoom-adaptive density, or the backing buffer reallocates on almost every frame.
Wrap attributes and divisors in a VAO so you never leave the map's shared GL state altered.
The globe recipe is not Three.js-specific — this layer hugs the sphere with hand-written GLSL.
limitations: The flow field is synthetic (a zonal base flow plus nine deterministic vortices), not meteorological data.
The field is constant; there is no hot-swapping a new frame of data while keeping particle history.
Particles respawn uniformly worldwide rather than biased toward the viewport, so high zoom wastes particles.

data.source: generated analytically at runtime, fixed seed
data.note: Continuous across the antimeridian and safe at the poles by construction: longitude only ever enters through sin/cos, which are exactly 2*pi periodic.

examples.title: Clicks on a layer that cannot be hit-tested
examples.settles: Interaction for custom layers. queryRenderedFeatures sees native layers only, and that is not a flag you can turn on.

knobs.effect: How a click is resolved. Both feed the same popup path, so the only difference is the search.
Screen-space only. Turn it off and every point on the far side of the planet becomes clickable.

teaches: The companion-layer trick: same data, circle-opacity 0, native layer owns interaction while the custom layer owns appearance.
map.project() is pure matrix arithmetic and returns a valid screen position for points behind the planet, so screen-space picking must cull the far side itself.
Read the camera ECEF the visual shader already computed rather than deriving it a second time and letting the two drift.
In the Mapbox style spec, ['zoom'] may only be the input to a top-level interpolate or step. Nesting it inside another expression is rejected at addLayer(), and TypeScript will not catch it.
limitations: The GPU ID-buffer strategy is described but not implemented.
Screen-space click tolerance is a fixed 14px rather than zoom-scaled.
The spatial grid is rebuilt on every click — fine at about 1k points, wrong at 100k.

examples.title: 68 procedural Three.js effects, with prompt templates
examples.settles: A browsable catalogue of visual techniques: geometry, lights, animation, shaders, particles, lines, data-viz forms, atmospherics, composed scenes.
examples.testsNote: No unit tests: every effect's build/update manipulates Three.js objects directly, with no pure functions worth isolating and nothing verifiable without a GPU.
usesApis: THREE geometries, materials, ShaderMaterial, Points, InstancedMesh

knobs.effect: Every effect exposes its own parameter sliders; the full set with ranges and defaults is in effects.json.

teaches: Each effect carries a filled-in prompt template — an instruction you can hand to an agent to reproduce that effect elsewhere.
effects.json gives id, category, title, description, tech, params, prompt and sourceFile for all 68.
limitations: 0 of 68 effects hug the globe. The gallery's shared layer never reads the globe render arguments, so every effect positions itself with a single absolute MercatorCoordinate. To put one on a sphere, apply docs/01-hugging-the-globe/mapbox.md.
Ported verbatim from an internal showcase: logic unchanged, only comments and display strings translated.
